issues: Dolphin body is filled with a heavy halftone/dither pattern, reading as static or noise rather than a smooth lit phosphor creature; the clean silhouette and rim light are lost in the speckle.
Dolphin is compressed into the top ~40% of the frame and oriented nearly horizontally, so it never becomes the arcing centerpiece occupying the middle 50-60% of display height.
The leap arc is weak: the body looks like a flat glide, the tail fluke is ambiguous, and the pectoral fin barely registers, hurting the graceful leaping pose.
The bottom third is over-busy: full-width FFT segments, the left VU meter, and right-side telemetry text together form a bright band that competes with the dolphin for attention.
Right-side metadata (128BPM, PHR 16/32, etc.) is not part of the reference OEL layout and pulls the eye away from the dolphin toward the corner.
Phosphor glow on the dolphin is flat because the dither breaks up the surface; there is no soft halo or back rim light to make it read as a glowing 3D object.
Scattered stray pixels around and below the dolphin read as random noise rather than intentional water splash or short persistence trails.
suggestions: Replace the halftone dither fill on the dolphin with a mostly solid phosphor fill plus a brighter 1px rim light along the back/head and a slightly dimmer interior, so the body reads as a lit, rounded creature instead of a noise field.

Enlarge the dolphin and shift it into the vertical center, raising its height to roughly 50-60% of the display, and strengthen the leap arc by lifting the tail and curving the spine into a clear crescent.

Sharpen the anatomy: a distinct triangular dorsal fin, a forked tail fluke, a visible pectoral fin, and a defined rostrum with a single eye pixel, all joined by smooth curves rather than blocky steps.
Dim the FFT bars and confine them to the bottom ~13% at low contrast, and remove or heavily dim the right-side telemetry text so the lower band stops competing with the dolphin.
Add a short, directional persistence trail fading behind the tail and pectoral fin to imply motion, keeping it 2-3 frames long so it never fogs the whole scene.
Apply a gentle bloom halo around the dolphin silhouette only, keeping the core edges crisp, to sell the authentic OEL phosphor glow without a whiteout.
Drop the water-surface lines to an even lower contrast and thinner stroke so they sit unambiguously beneath and behind the dolphin as a subordinate layer.
